content: The North America Society (NASPGHAN) and the Pan Arab Society (PASPGHAN) conducted a survey involving 142 healthcare workers. Among these, 94 had treated children or adolescents infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) in the past three years. Respondents represented all WHO geographic regions, with the highest proportions from the Western Pacific (43%) and the Americas (19%). However, the survey did not include end-users such as parents, caregivers, or the children themselves, as routine testing and case identification for children remain limited. Consequently, most parents are unaware of their child’s infection, and even fewer have experience with their child receiving treatment. Regarding treatment preferences for different age groups, 94% of respondents strongly supported treating adolescents aged 12–17 years, 81% supported treating children aged 6–11 years, and 60% supported treating children aged 3–5 years. The most common reasons cited for not treating younger children included the possibility of spontaneous viral clearance (27%), slower disease progression and asymptomatic nature in early childhood (24%), limited clinical trial data (15%), lack of drug approvals for direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens in younger age groups (22%), and difficulties in administering medication to young children (12%). A majority of respondents (59%) supported including treatment recommendations for children aged three years and older in clinical guidelines. An additional 15% supported recommendations for children aged six years and older, while 22% supported treatment for adolescents only. The most commonly used and preferred DAA regimens among healthcare workers with recent treatment experience were sofosbuvir/ledipasvir (52% for adolescents, 28% for older children), sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (32% for adolescents, 20% for older children), and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (23% for adolescents, 10% for older children). The primary reason for their use, cited by 95% of respondents, was drug availability at their facilities. Other reasons included good safety data (95%), professional society guidelines recommending their use (88%), suitability for treating prevalent HCV genotypes (84%), and high efficacy (72%). Although no survey of end-users (parents or HCV-infected children/adolescents) was conducted, previous studies indicate that short-course (8–12 weeks) oral DAA treatment is highly acceptable to adolescents, children, and their caregivers due to its high likelihood of cure and minimal adverse effects compared to interferon injections. Achieving a cure allows children and adolescents to live free of the stigma associated with HCV infection. However, younger children may face challenges with medication palatability, especially if the medication is only available in tablet form, such as sofosbuvir/daclatasvir. The approval of DAAs for use in adolescents and younger children represents a significant opportunity to expand treatment access and achieve cures for a vulnerable population that benefits from early intervention. With 26 million children globally living with chronic HCV infection, national elimination of HCV will not be possible unless children and adolescents are also tested and treated. Equitable access to recommended DAAs must be ensured for all HCV-infected children and adolescents, including those from stigmatized populations such as people who inject drugs and men who have sex with men. A systematic review reported treatment experience among 2,906 adolescents and children (2,228 adolescents aged 12–18 years, 472 older children aged 6–11 years, and 167 young children aged 3–5 years) using various DAA regimens, including sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, and sofosbuvir/ledipasvir. Overall, efficacy was high, and no major adverse effects were reported. Regulatory approval for sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for children as young as three years was granted in 2021. Pharmacokinetic modeling suggests that existing adult doses of sofosbuvir/daclatasvir (400 mg/60 mg) are safe and effective for children weighing at least 25 kg, with half doses (200 mg/30 mg) suitable for those weighing 14–25 kg. However, evidence for certain genotypes, such as genotype 4r common in sub-Saharan Africa, remains uncertain. The national scale-up of testing and treatment among school-age children and adolescents in Egypt has demonstrated the feasibility and acceptability of case-finding and treatment among children and their caregivers. However, pediatric-specific dosage forms are more expensive than adult tablets due to smaller commercial markets, which attract limited interest from generic suppliers. The most efficient approach to developing generic pediatric dosage forms is to scale down adult products, such as using scored tablets or half-dose separate tablets. Gilead and AbbVie received US FDA approval in 2021 for the use of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir in children as young as three years. However, these originator products are expensive and unlikely to be available at the scale needed for children in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir is considered the most appropriate pangenotypic option for optimizing access in LMICs due to its wide availability, low cost, and equivalent safety and efficacy for common genotypes 1 and 4. However, treatment failure may occur with certain genotypes, such as HCV genotype 4 non-a/d subtypes and others with resistance-associated substitutions in the NS5A region. Pharmacokinetic modeling data suggest that a dosage of daclatasvir 30 mg and sofosbuvir 200 mg (half the adult dose) provides appropriate drug exposure for younger children. However, sofosbuvir in 100 mg or 200 mg dosage forms to pair with daclatasvir is not yet available, and urgent advocacy is needed to promote the development of a 100 mg sofosbuvir dosage. Sofosbuvir 100 mg or 200 mg is now included on the 2022 WHO pre-qualification list, and daclatasvir 30 mg has been included since 2016. Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir remains substantially less expensive than other regimens, with benchmark pricing for a 12-week treatment course as low as $25 in Pakistan and $48 in Egypt. Aligning adult and pediatric regimens allows for centralized pooled procurement, larger volumes, and lower prices, as well as streamlined supply chain management and simplified service delivery. All recommended DAA regimens for children and adolescents (sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) were included in the 2021 update to the WHO Essential Medicines List for Children (EMLc). To maximize effectiveness, HCV treatment programs for children and adolescents should be aligned and integrated with adult programs, recognizing the differences in caregivers. National plans and guidelines should include case-finding, testing, care, and treatment for children and adolescents. However, few LMICs currently include adolescents and children in their national viral hepatitis strategies, leaving most cases undiagnosed and untreated. Testing strategies should prioritize children of HCV-positive mothers, especially if co-infected with HIV, and consider offering testing to children and adolescents attending HIV, STI, or TB clinics or admitted to hospitals in high-prevalence regions. Testing should also be offered to children presenting with symptoms of acute viral hepatitis. Raising awareness among healthcare workers and the public about the need for screening and the availability of curative treatments is essential. Non-specialist pediatricians can treat HCV-infected children and adolescents, but cases involving cirrhosis or prior DAA treatment failure may require specialist supervision.
